summary: This note is a clipped Wikipedia article on earthquakes, covering their definition, causes along faults and volcanoes, fault types, energy release and magnitude, and the seismic waves they generate. It also surveys major historical events such as the 1556 Shaanxi and 1960 Valdivia earthquakes, the frequency of earthquakes worldwide, and induced seismicity. The excerpt ends partway through the section on seismic wave speeds, so later sections on effects, management and culture are not included.
one_line: Wikipedia overview of earthquakes: their causes along faults, fault types, magnitude and energy, seismic waves, and notable historical events.
key_facts: An earthquake is the shaking of the Earth's surface resulting from a sudden release of energy in the lithosphere that creates seismic waves.
The initial point of rupture of an earthquake is called its hypocenter or focus, and the epicenter is the ground point directly above it.
The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake occurred on 23 January 1556 in Shaanxi, China, and more than 830,000 people died.
The 1960 Chilean earthquake reached 9.5 magnitude on 22 May 1960 and is the largest earthquake measured on a seismograph.
The 1976 Tangshan earthquake killed between 240,000 and 655,000 people and was the deadliest of the 20th century.
For every unit increase in magnitude there is a roughly thirty-fold increase in energy released.
An 8.6-magnitude earthquake releases the same amount of energy as 10,000 atomic bombs of the size used in World War II.
Megathrust earthquakes on reverse faults are responsible for about 90% of the total seismic moment released worldwide.
Normal faults are generally associated with earthquakes less than magnitude 7, because many lie along spreading centers such as in Iceland.
It is estimated that around 500,000 earthquakes occur each year that are detectable with current instrumentation, and about 100,000 of these can be felt.
Most of the world's earthquakes (90%, and 81% of the largest) take place in the circum-Pacific seismic belt, known as the Pacific Ring of Fire.
The 5.7 magnitude 2011 Oklahoma earthquake is thought to have been caused by disposing wastewater from oil production into injection wells.
Elastic-rebound theory describes the gradual build-up of strain and stress punctuated by occasional sudden earthquake failure.
The 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes ruptured along segments of the East Anatolian Fault at supershear speeds, and more than 50,000 people died in both countries.
Earthquake swarms differ from aftershock sequences because no single earthquake in the swarm is notably larger than the others, as in the 2004 activity at Yellowstone National Park.

entities.name: Shaanxi earthquake (1556)
entities.role: One of the most devastating earthquakes in recorded history, in Shaanxi, China, with more than 830,000 deaths

entities.name: Tangshan earthquake (1976)
entities.role: The deadliest earthquake of the 20th century, killing between 240,000 and 655,000 people

entities.name: 1960 Chilean earthquake
entities.role: Largest earthquake measured on a seismograph, reaching 9.5 magnitude on 22 May 1960 near Cañete, Chile

entities.name: Good Friday earthquake
entities.role: Earthquake of 27 March 1964 centered in Prince William Sound, Alaska, whose energy was about half that of the 1960 Chilean earthquake

entities.name: 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake
entities.role: One of the ten largest recorded earthquakes and also one of the deadliest in history

entities.name: 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes
entities.role: Earthquakes that ruptured the East Anatolian Fault at supershear speeds, killing more than 50,000 people in both countries

entities.name: 2011 Oklahoma earthquake
entities.role: 5.7 magnitude earthquake thought to be caused by wastewater disposal from oil production

entities.name: 2008 Sichuan earthquake
entities.role: 8.0 magnitude earthquake that a Columbia University paper suggested was induced by loading from the Zipingpu Dam

entities.name: 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens
entities.role: Volcanic eruption preceded by earthquakes that served as an early warning

entities.name: Messina earthquake and tsunami
entities.role: Event of 28 December 1908 that took almost 100,000 lives in Sicily and Calabria

entities.name: 1896 Sanriku earthquake
entities.role: Example of a tsunami earthquake whose low felt intensities failed to alert the neighboring coast

entities.name: 2001 Kunlun earthquake
entities.role: Supershear earthquake whose unusually wide zone of damage has been attributed to a sonic boom effect

entities.name: San Andreas Fault
entities.role: Strike-slip fault cited for the 1857 and 1906 earthquakes

entities.name: Parkfield, California
entities.role: Location of a long-term research study around an earthquake cluster

entities.name: Iceland
entities.role: Spreading center where the brittle layer is only about six kilometres thick, limiting normal fault magnitudes

entities.name: Yellowstone National Park
entities.role: Site of the 2004 earthquake swarm

entities.name: Pacific Ring of Fire
entities.role: Horseshoe-shaped zone where most of the world's earthquakes occur and which bounds the Pacific Plate

entities.name: Charles Francis Richter
entities.role: Developed the first scale for measuring earthquake magnitudes in 1935

entities.name: Richter magnitude scale
entities.role: Instrumental scale first developed in the 1930s, whose use has become minimal in the 21st century

entities.name: Moment magnitude scale
entities.role: Scale standard practice uses to express earthquake strength, based on the static seismic moment

entities.name: United States Geological Survey (USGS)
entities.role: Agency that estimates earthquake averages and publishes detailed statistics on earthquake size and frequency

entities.name: Gutenberg–Richter law
entities.role: Law describing the exponential relationship between earthquake frequency and magnitude, illustrated by UK recurrence rates

entities.name: Elastic-rebound theory
entities.role: Theory describing the build-up and sudden release of strain that causes earthquakes

entities.name: Circum-Pacific seismic belt
entities.role: Horseshoe-shaped zone of about 40,000 km where most of the world's earthquakes take place
